OPINIONS BELOW
The opinion of the court of appeals ( J.A. 1-47) is
available  at 2026 WL 2797801 .  The opinion of the district court ( J.A. 48-150) is reported  at 821 F.  Supp. 3d
102.
JURISDICTION
The judgment of the court of appeals was entered on
September 18 , 2026.  On September 29, 2026, this Court
treated the government’s application for a stay as a petition for a writ of certiorari, and granted the petition.
The jurisdiction of this Court rests on 28 U.S.C. 1254(1).
CONSTITUTIONAL, STATUTORY , AND REGULATORY
PROVISIONS INVOLVED
Pertinent provisions are reproduced in the appendix
to this brief .  App., infra, 1a-67a.

2

INTRODUCTION
The rules governing removal of aliens from this
country are a sovereign pre rogative largely committed
to the political branches.   Congress has granted the Executive significant discretion in selecting the country to
which an alien with a final order of removal will be
sent—including a “third countr y” that is authorized by
statute but not identified in  the removal order.  A nd
while the United States has accepted certain humanitarian responsibilities not to remove an alien to a country where it determines he will likely face torture o r
certain forms of persecution, Congress did not specify
procedures to make that determination in the context of
third-country removals, leaving th e matter to the Executive’s broad discretion.   In addition , Congress has imposed stringent bars on judicial review of legal questions arising from the Executive’s actions taken to execute removal orders.
In March 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a policy adopting a two -track process
for determining whether an alien selected  for removal
to a third country is likely to face torture or persecution
there.  For countries that have given the United States
diplomatic assurance s deemed credible that no aliens
will be tortured or persecuted upon removal there, DHS
will treat those assurance s as conclusive .  For countries
without such assurance s, the alien will receive actual
notice of the proposed country and a n opportunity for a
prompt screening of any asserted fear of removal  there.
That policy solved a serious problem that had long
plagued this Nation.  The United States is often unable
to remov e aliens to their home countries —whether because they have been granted protection from removal
there, or because those countries refuse to accept them

3

for various reasons , including that many of them have
serious criminal histories.   Absent a viable system for
third-country removals, such aliens often were released.  That gave such aliens a compelling, perverse incentive to raise meritless fear -based claims.  It also inflicted predictable and tragic consequences , as criminal
aliens—including class members here who have been
convicted of murder, armed robbery, sexual assault of
minors and the mentally disabled, and more —have ravaged American communities.  See D. Ct. Doc. 129 -1, at
1-9 (May 23, 2025) .  The policy fixes th ose longstanding
failures, while also accounting for our humanitarian obligations.   And its directive to remove aliens swiftly once
a third country is identified is essential , as finding a
willing country often entails delicate diplomatic negotiations that would be undermined by lengthy delays .  See
C.A. Doc. 118413581, at 3 -4 (Mar. 5, 2026) .
The decision s below jeopardize all of that.  The lower
courts invalidate d the policy on the grounds that the immigration laws and the Constitution  require greater notice and opportunity to raise claims that an alien will be
persecuted or tortured  in the third country selected by
DHS.  But the relevant statutes and regulations say
nothing about procedures to evaluate such claims in the
context of third-country removals.  The lower courts insisted that the notice -and-opportunity procedures  that
they demanded  were “implicit” in those authorities.
But vague due-process concerns do not license courts to
engraft new procedures on plain text, or to augment the
procedures that the Executive has adopted to aid its
own decision about whether an alien will face maltreatment abroad .  At any rate, there is no due-process problem here .  To the extent that the Constitution entitles
aliens to any process beyond what the political branches

4

provide—which it does not for the many class members
who never obtained admission to this country in the first
place—the policy’s two-track scheme easily meets the
minimal requirements of the Due Process Clause in this
context  where deference to the Executive is at its acme .
In all events , under the Immigration and Nationality
Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq., the courts below clearly
lacked jurisdiction  even to reach the  merits.  Congress
specifically decreed that no district court “shall have jurisdiction ” over “any cause or claim ” “arising from the
decision or action ” to “execute removal orders against
any alien. ”  8 U.S.C. 1252(g).  And Congress  more generally provided that “no court shall have jurisdiction” to
review “questions of law and fact” “arising from any action taken” to “remove an alien,” except through a petition for review of a final removal order.  8  U.S.C.
1252(b)(9).  Congress also expressly preclude d district -
court jurisdiction over any claims “under” the Convention Against Torture .  8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(4 ).  The lower
courts improperly disregarded all of those jurisdictional
bars by inventing atextual limitations  and invoking
practical  concerns.
At a minimum, t he lower courts violated  the INA’s
bar on classwide remedies that “enjoin or restrain” the
operation of the statute’s removal provisions .  8 U.S.C.
1252(f  )(1).  They tried to end -run that bar  by framing
the relief as a series of declaratory judgments and a universal vacatur of the policy , rather than as a permanent
injunction .  But the “enjoin or restrain” language covers
coercive declarations that invite follow-on injunctions,
for lower courts may not do in two steps what they are
barred from doing in one.  So too for the vacatur, which
likewise restrains agency officials from  implementing
the policy’s third -country-removal procedures .

5

This Court has stayed three attempts by the lower
courts to halt the challenged policy .  It should now definitively  allow the policy to remain in effect .  The policy
marks the considered judgment of the Executive
Branch about how best to fulfill its humanitarian obligations while also finally facilitating the removal of aliens who have been able to avoid removal (sometimes
for years ), often because of their dangerousness .  The
lower courts had no jurisdictional authority or merits
basis to set aside the policy, much less fashion their own
process that achieves only delay and obstruction .  While
the aliens at issue may benefit from stalling their removal even further, the Nation does not.
STATEMENT
A. Background
1. The INA authorizes the removal of classes of aliens from the United States.  See, e.g., 8 U.S.C. 1182 (a),
1227(a), 1231 (a).  The removal process can include a
hearing before an immigration judge, an appeal to the
Board of Immigration Appeals  (BIA), and a petition for
review in a court of appeals.  See 8 U.S.C. 1229a,
1252(a).  Many aliens facing removal have an opportunity to apply for relief or protection from removal.
See, e.g., 8 U.S.C. 1158 (asylum).
Congress also has established a n expedited -removal
system for certain aliens.  See 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(1).  Under that  system, certain inadmissible aliens receive
speedy administrative review of any asserted fears of
persecution in the country to which they will be removed; they are not entitled to judicial review of an adverse administrative determination.  See DHS v.
Thuraissigiam , 591 U.S. 103, 109-113 (2020).  Congress
further  has established streamlined process es for removing certain aliens convicted of  aggravated felonies

6

and for reinstating removal orders against aliens who
unlawfully reenter the country after having been removed.  See 8 U.S.C. 1228(b), 1231(a)(5).
2. The INA establishes  a sequence and  criteria for
the government to determin e the country to which an
alien will be removed.  8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(1) and (2) .1  Possible destinations include a country designated by the
alien, the alien ’s country of citizenship, and the alien ’s
previous country of residence.  See Jama v. ICE, 543
U.S. 335, 338-341 (2005) .  But the Executive retains
broad discretion  about where to send an alien , as it may
generally decline to send an alien to listed countries
on grounds like impracticability or prejudice to national
interests.  See, e.g., 8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(1)(C)(iv)  and
(2)(E)(vii) .  Section 1231(b) thus offers a fail-safe option:
any other country whose government “will accept the
alien.”  Ibid.  Such countries may be selected even if not
identified in an alien ’s removal order.  See 8  C.F.R.
1240.12(d).
Congress also has provided two means for an alien to
challenge removal to a country where he may face persecution or torture.  First, an alien may seek withholding of removal under 8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3).  Statutory
withholding generally prohibits removing an alien to a
country if the government determines that he would
face persecution there because of his “race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or
political opinion. ”  8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3)(A).  Second, the
alien may seek protection  under regulations implementing the Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel,
Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment

1  The statute refers to the Attorney General, but Congress transferred enforcement of certain INA provisions to the Secretary of
Homeland Security.  Nielsen v. Preap, 586 U.S. 392, 397 n.2 (2019).

7

(CAT), adopted Dec. 10, 1984, S. Treaty Doc. No. 20,
100th Cong., 2d Sess. (1988), 1465 U.N.T.S. 85 —a non -
self-executing treaty  under which state parties agreed
not to return a person to a country where there is substantial danger the individual would be tortured.  See
Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998
(FARRA), Pub. L. No. 105 -277, Div. G, §  2242(b), 112
Stat. 2681 -822 (statute directing Executive to implement CAT by regulation) ; 8  C.F.R. 208.16-208.18,
1208.16 -1208.18.
Ordinarily, an alien raises a withholding or CAT
claim during removal proceedings, where the immigration judge decides both the alien ’s removability and
claims for protection  from removal.  See, e.g., 8 C.F.R.
1240.1(a)(1)(iii), 1240.12(c).  But withholding and CAT
claims can  also arise outside of those proceedings.  For
example, an alien subject to a reinstated order of removal may seek  “withholding -only” relief.  Riley v.
Bondi, 606 U.S. 259, 265 (2025).  And an alien subject to
expedited removal may raise a fear of persecution or
torture.  See Thuraissigiam , 591 U.S. at 110 n.5.
Statutory withholding and CAT protection affect
only where, not whether, an alien may be removed.  See
Johnson  v. Guzman Chavez , 594 U.S. 523, 536 (2021) .
When an alien receives such country -specific protection, the government “retains the authority to remove
the alien to any other country authorized by [ Section
1231(b)],” because the removal order “remains in full
force.”  Ibid.  The statute and regulations do not set
forth any particular procedure s the government must
follow in making withholding or CAT determinations in
the specific context of third -country removals .
3. On President Trump ’s first day  back in office, he
determined that the millions of aliens who have illegally

8

crossed the border pose a serious threat to national security.  Exec. Order No. 14,165, 90 Fed. Reg. 8467 (Jan.
30, 2025).  The President  thus directed  DHS to take “all
appropriate actions ” to detain and remove aliens who
have been ordered removed, but who nevertheless have
been “released into the United States. ”  Id. at 8468.  In
February 2025, DHS issued guidance directing U.S.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to review cases of aliens who had been ordered removed, but
whose removal was impeded .  J.A. 207.  DHS directed
ICE to, inter alia , “determine the viability of removal
to a third country ” for such aliens, especially “in light of
the Administration ’s significant gains with regard to
previously recalcitrant countries. ”  Ibid.
Such third -country removals  are not uncommon.
Sometimes the countries identified  in a removal order
are no t viable options by the time DHS is prepared to
remove the alien.   For example, countries are often reluctant to accept murderers, rapists,  sexual abusers,
and other violent felons, even if they are from that country.  See D. Ct. Doc. 129 -1, at 1 -9 (collecting examples
of criminal aliens  not promptly removed ).  Or an alien
may obtain withholding or CAT protection  from the
only country listed in his removal order.  In such instances , third-country removal is the only way for DHS
to exercise its “authority” under Section 1231(b) to execute final  removal order s.  See 8  C.F.R. 1240.12(d).
And as a practical matter, that third country often falls
within Section 1231(b) ’s catch-all provisions allowing removal to any country willing to accept the alien.
On March 30, 2025, DHS clarified its “policy regarding the removal of aliens with final orders of removal
pursuant to sections 240, 241(a)(5), or 238(b) of the
[INA] to countries other than those designated for re-

9

moval in those removal orders. ”  J.A. 30 6; see J.A. 306 -
309.2  A substantially similar memo on July 9 affirmed
that policy  (together with the March memo, the Guidance).  J.A. 31 0-313.  The Guidance distinguishes between countries that have provided credible assurances
that any aliens removed there will not be persecuted or
tortured, and countries that have not.
For countries that have provided such assurances,
“the alien may be removed without the need for further
procedures. ”  J.A. 307, 311.  For countries that have not,
DHS first provides actual notice to  the alien of the country of removal (read to him in a language he understands)  and give s him an opportunity to “affirmatively
express a fear of persecution or torture ” there.  J.A.
308.  DHS “will generally wait at least 24 hours following service of the Notice of Removal before effectuating
removal. ”  J.A. 31 1.  If an alien express es such a fear
about the country of removal , an asylum officer will conduct a prompt screening to determine whether he
“would more likely than not be ” persecuted or tortured
there.  J.A. 31 2.  If the alien fails to satisfy that standard, he “will be removed. ”  Ibid.  If he does satisfy it, he
will be put into additional administrative procedures,
consistent with how withholding and CAT claims typically are handled.  J.A. 31 2-313.  “Alternatively, ICE
may choose to designate another country for removal ”
and start the process afresh.  J.A. 313.

241(a)(5) is 8  U.S.C. 1231(a)(5) (“Reinstatement of removal orders
against aliens illegally reentering”); and Section 238(b) is 8  U.S.C.
1228(b) (expedited “[r]emoval of aliens who are not permanent residents” and convicted of an aggravated felony ).

10

B. Proceedings Below
1. Respondents are four aliens subject to final orders of removal.  J.A. 227-230.  In March 2025, they filed
this putative class action, alleging that there are “valid
reasons to fear removal to specific countries that were
not included in their removal orders. ”  J.A. 230 .  Each
respondent claim ed, among other things, that due process requires additional “notice and an opportunity to
be heard prior to removal to a country that was not designated in their removal orders. ”  Ibid.
In April 2025, the district court granted respondents ’
motion for class certification and issued a classwide preliminary injunction.  J.A. 219-279.3  After concluding it
had jurisdiction, including to issue classwide relief, the
court held that the Guidance likely violated due process
because it did not provide “notice and a meaningful opportunity to present fear -based claims ” under CAT.
J.A. 265; see J.A. 265 -273, 278 n.51 .  The court ordered
DHS to ( 1) provide written notice to aliens and counsel
of the third country to which they might be removed;
(2) provide aliens with a “meaningful opportunity ” to assert a fear of removal; ( 3) use a “reasonable fear ” standard, rather than a “more likely than not ” standard , to
assess the credibility of those assertions; and ( 4) pro-

All individuals who have a final removal order issued in proceedings under Section 240, 241(a)(5), or 238(b) of the INA (including

deport on or after February 18, 2025, to a country (a) not previously designated as the country or alternative country of removal, and (b) not identified in writing in the prior proceedings
as a country to which the individual would be removed.
J.A. 247.

11

vide dissatisfied aliens at least 15 days to “move to reopen immigration proceedings. ”  J.A. 276 -277 & n.48.
In May 2025, the district court “clarif [ied]” that the
injunction ’s reference to a “meaningful opportunity ” to
“raise a fear -based claim ” meant “a minimum of ten
days.”  J.A. 285 (emphasis omitted).  The court ordered
various remedial measures, including that each alien
“be given a reasonable fear interview in private ”; that
“counsel of their choosing [be] present ”; that the alien
and his counsel “be given no fewer than 72 -hours’ notice
of the scheduled time for each reasonable fear interview”; and that the government provide periodic status
reports to the court.  J.A. 287-288.
The Secretary of State explained that the injunction
would “cause significant and irreparable harm to U.S.
foreign policy” by undermining delicate diplomatic negotiations with third countries to accept these aliens.
D. Ct. Doc. 130 -1, at 2 , ¶ 3 (May 23, 2025).  And ICE
explained that the court -ordered delays would disrupt
and thus effectively prevent third-country removal operations, which often involve “significant logistical difficulties” to coordinate flights, pilots, crews , country
clearances, and foreign law -enforcement across multiple countries.  D.  Ct. Doc. 130 -2, at 8, ¶  24 (May 23,
2025); see id. at 8-10, ¶¶ 26-28.
2. On June 23, 2025, this Court stayed the preliminary injunction in full.  145 S. Ct. 2153 (No. 24A1153).
Later that same evening, the district court issued an order asserting that its May remedial order “remains in
full force and effect, notwithstanding today ’s stay of the
Preliminary Injunction. ”  D. Ct. Docket Entry No. 176.
On July 3, 2025, this Court granted the government ’s
motion to clarify that the June 23 stay of the prelimi-

12

nary injunction necessarily barred the district court
from enforcing that injunction.  145 S. Ct. 2627.
The district court then granted respondents ’ motion
for an indicative ruling that it would “dissolve the preliminary injunction if the First Circuit remanded [the]
appeal for that purpose. ”  D. Ct. Doc. 212 , at 4 (Aug. 28,
2025).  The court of appeals remanded the case, D.  Ct.
Doc. 239 (Feb. 20, 2026) , and the district court dissolved
the preliminary injunction, J.A. 67.
3. In February 2026, t he district court issued a final
judgment granting summary judgment to respondents
on their claims that the Guidance violates the Due Process Clause and 8  U.S.C. 1231(b), while dismissing the
remaining counts.  J.A. 48 -150.  As relevant , the court
held that it had jurisdiction,  that the INA does not preclude classwide coercive relief, and that the Guidance
violates both due process  and Section 1231(b) because it
does not provide class members adequate notice or opportunity to raise withholding or CAT claims before being removed to a third country .  J.A. 149-150.
The district court declared DHS ’s “third-country removal policy, as embodied in ” the Guidance, to be “unlawful, ” and universally vacated that policy.  J.A. 152.
Relevant here, the court declared that class members
have the right “to meaningful notice before removal to
any third country ” and “to a meaningful opportunity to
raise a country -specific claim against removal before removal to any third country. ”  Ibid.
5. The First Circuit granted a stay pending appeal,
C.A. Doc. 118417272  (Mar. 16, 2026) , but in September
2026, it affirmed the district court ’s judgment  in relevant part, J.A. 1 -47.  The court of appeals adopted the
district court ’s jurisdictional and remedial analyses,
J.A. 14 -27, 42-46; and it agreed that Section 1231(b) re-

13

quires notice and an opportunity to raise statutory withholding claims before a third -country removal, J.A. 30-
37.  The court  of appeals declined to hold the Guidance
unconstitutional  (unlike the district court ), but invoked
the same considerations to hold  that, under constitutional avoidance, FARRA itself imposes the same procedural requirements for CAT claims.  J.A. 37-42.
6. After the First Circuit dissolved its stay pending
appeal, C.A. Doc. 118513248  (Sept. 23, 2026), this Court
stayed the district court’s order, treated the government’s stay application as a petition for a writ of certiorari, and granted the petition.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
I. The district court lacked jurisdiction over respondents’ claims .  8 U.S.C. 1252(g)  specifically provides that no district court “shall have jurisdiction” over
“any cause or claim” “arising from the decision or action” to “execute removal orders against any alien.”
The lower courts misread Section 1252(g) as limited to
challenges to the government’s exercise of discretion,
not its authority.  But that limitation has no basis in the
text and would render the statute  effectively toothless,
as it is easy to restyle any challenge to the government’s
discretion as a challenge to its authority.
In addition, 8  U.S.C. 1252(b)(9) more generally provides that “no court shall have jurisdiction” to review
any “questions of law and fact” “arising from any action
taken” to “remove an alien,” except through a petition
for review of a final removal order.  Whether the government’s procedures for removing aliens to third countries are adequate is a question of law and fact arising
from actions taken to remove those aliens.  The lower
courts’ practical concerns with that conclusion  cannot
override th e plain statutory text.

14

Section 2242(d) of FARRA and 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(4)
further  preclude district -court jurisdiction over claims
“under” CAT , which includes respondents’ statutory
and constitutional  claims based on CAT .  The lower
courts’ contrary reasoning that a claim is only “under”
a statute providing the cause of action would nullify
these jurisdictional bars, because CAT and FARRA
provide no cause of action at all.
II.  The district court lacked authority to enter classwide relief under 8 U.S.C. 1252(f  )(1), which strips lower
federal courts of authority  to “enjoin or restrain the operation” of the INA’s removal provisions  on a classwide
basis.  That language covers coercive declaratory judgments that inhibit how the defendant may act and invite
follow-on injunctions to enforce compliance .  This Court
has interpreted  similar statutory language to encompass coercive declaratory relief, e.g., California  v.
Grace Brethren  Church, 457 U.S. 393, 408 (1982) , which
defeats the lower courts’ emphasis on the lack of an explicit reference to declaratory relief.  For the same reasons, Section 1252(f  )(1) also bars the universal vacatur
here, which “check[s], hold[s] back, or prevent[s]”
agency officials from carrying out third-country removals under the Guidance .  Garland  v. Aleman Gonzalez ,
596 U.S. 543, 549 (2022).  That was the entire point .
III.  In all events , the Guidance is lawful.  It does not
violate any statutory or regulatory provision because
neither Section 1231 nor FARRA  (nor their implementing regulations)  sets forth specific procedures for third -
country removals at all .  Indeed, filling that gap was the
reason for the policy.  The Guidance also comports with
due process.  It ensures that any alien will either be sent
to a country where the United States has secured a
credible assurance that no alien will be tortured or per-

15

secuted, or will be given actual notice and a n opportunity for a prompt review as to any affirmative fear of
removal.  Whatever the Due Process Clause may require in this context  involving immig ration and foreign
affairs —where the Executive is entitled to the greatest
deference —it demands no more than that .
ARGUMENT
I. THE DISTRICT COURT LACKED JURISDICTION OVER
RESPONDENTS’ CLAIMS
Respondents  challenge their removals to third countries under valid removal orders on the ground that the
government must afford them more process before executing those removals.  But the INA precludes district -
court jurisdiction over , among other things,  “any”
claims “arising from” the “decision or action” to “execute removal orders,” 8 U.S.C. 1252(g), as well as “all”
questions “arising from” an “action taken or proceeding
brought to remove an alien,” 8  U.S.C. 1252(b)(9) .  Those
jurisdictional  bars unambiguously cover respondents’
claims.  And the CAT-related claims are also covered by
CAT-specific jurisdictional bars .  8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(4);
FARRA §  2242(d), 112 Stat. 2681 -822.
A. Section 1252(g) Preclude s Jurisdiction
1. The INA specifically prohibits district courts
from exercising jurisdiction over suits like this one that
challeng e actions taken to execute removal orders.  It
states that , “[e]xcept as provided in this section and notwithstanding any other provision of law (statutory or
nonstatutory),   * * *  no court shall have jurisdiction to
hear any cause or claim by or on behalf of any alien arising from the decision or action by the [government]  to
commence proceedings, adjudicate cases, or execute removal orders against any alien .”  8 U.S.C. 1252(g).

16

Section 1252(g)  clearly covers respondents’ claims.
Respondents challenge the country to which they are to
be removed because the government ’s procedures for
determining th at country are supposedly deficient.  A
claim about where an alien will be removed is, ipso
facto, a “claim” “arising from the decision or action ” to
“execute [a] removal order[] .”  8 U.S.C. 1252(g) .
To “execute” a removal order means to “perform ” or
“complete” the removal .  Black’s Law Dictionary  567
(6th ed. 1990).  And “the decision” to perform or complete the removal, 8 U.S.C. 1252(g),  necessarily includes
deciding whether, when, and where to remove the alien.
That includes removal to a third country  not identified
in the order, which incorporates “the authority of
[DHS] to remove the alien to any other country as permitted by [ Section 1231(b)].”  8  C.F.R. 1240.12(d).   At a
minimum, identifying a third country is an “action” to
perform or complete the removal order ed, and respondents’ claims “aris[e] from” that action.  8 U.S.C. 1252(g).
If the government were not executing an alien’s removal order , the alien would not even be a member of
the class here, much less have standing to challenge the
Guidance.  See J.A. 247.  Similarly , the relief entered
bars the government from continuing to execute removal orders through third -country removals without
engaging in the district court’s added procedures .  See
J.A. 152.  That confirms that each class member ’s claim
arises from the government ’s actions to execute his removal order.
That plain-text conclusion also follows directly from
Reno v. American -Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, 525 U.S. 471 (1999) ( AADC).  The Court there emphasized that, while Section 1252(g) does not “cover[]
the universe of deportation claims,”  it does apply to the

A. Section 1252(f  )(1) Prohibits Coercive Declarations

“caption and text  *  * *  reference only injunctions.”
J.A. 43.  But Section 1252(f  )(1) forbids lower courts  “to

2. The First Circuit “emphasized that a declaratory
judgment is a ‘milder remedy’ than an injunction ” because “it does not coerce a party, prohibit any future
action, or ‘set the stage for a finding of contempt.’  ”  J.A.
43.  But that wrongly treats all declaratory judgments
the same.  Some declaratory judgments are not coercive, such as those that clarify whether the plaintiff  may
act (or not act) in a certain way, e.g., MedImmune, Inc.
v. Genentech, Inc. , 549 U.S. 118, 130 (2007) (patent licensee may seek declaration on patent ’s invalidity), or
those that declare a policy unlawful but “in [their]
agreed substance d[o] not contemplate injunctive relief,” Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez , 372 U.S. 144, 155
(1963) ( government allowed to continue enforcing stat-

27

act (or not act) in a certain way and that contemplates a
follow-on injunction  to enforce compliance does check,
hold back, and prevent the defendant, and thus has the
practical effect of an injunction.  That is the case here.

enforceable “right” to “meaningful notice ” and “meaningful opportunity ” to be heard before they can be removed to a third country.  J.A. 152.  It thus  invites

A. The Guidance Does Not Violate Section  1231(b)
The First Circuit held that Section 1231(b) requires
the government to provide aliens “with effective notice
and a meaningful opportunity to raise any fear -of-
persecution claim before a third -country removal,” and
that the Guidance fail s to do so.  J.A. 30.  The court presumably would demand what the district court mandated in its preliminary injunction under the same
“meaningful” standard —10 days to raise a fear of removal and 15 days to challenge any adverse finding.  See
J.A. 285, 288.  Regardless of the precise details, no such
requirements exist under Section 1231(b) .
1. By its terms, Section 1231(b) does not mandate
any procedural requirements for assessing whether removal to a third country should be withheld  based on a
fear of persecution .  To be sure, it forbids the government, subject to certain exceptions,  from “remov[ing]
an alien to a country  if the [government] decides  that
the alien’s life or freedom would be threatened  in that
country” on certain grounds.  8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3)(A)
(emphasis added) .  But Section 1231(b)(3) is generally
silent on the procedures the government must employ
in making withholding  decision s, and  there is no language imposing a notice-and-opportunity requirement
of the type invented by the courts below .
When Congress entrusts an agency with “responsibility for substantive judgments,” and does not specify
the procedures for making that judgment, it presumptively also entrusts the agency with “the formulation of
[such] procedures.”  Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power
Corp. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. , 435
U.S. 519, 524 (1978).  While the Executive has adopted
regulations governing withholding claims in various
contexts, e.g., 8 C.F.R. 208.16 , 1208.16, none of them ad-

32

dresses the procedures for making withholding determinations in the context of third -country removals.  Cf.
J.A. 307 n.2.  Thus, the Executive has  discretion to fill
that regulatory gap, which DHS exercised through the
Guidance.  See FCC v. Brown, No. 26A476  (Oct. 14,
2026) (per curiam) , slip op. 3 -4.
All the more so because Congress makes clear when
it wishes to impose specific immigration procedures.
See, e.g., 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(1)(B)(iii)(III) (requiring government to “provide by regulation” a hearing before an
immigration judge  for the “review” of certain  “credible
fear” determinations).  But Section 1231 contains no
such directive  applicable here , let alone one resembling

the First Circuit acknowledged that the procedural requirements it imposed appear nowhere in the statute’s
express text, and instead had to be “read[]” “into” the
provision by  “constru[ing ]” Section 1231(b)(3) to “mean
more than what [it] plainly say[s] .”  J.A. 33.  That is sufficient basis to reverse under Vermont Yankee .
2. In fact, Section 1231 expressly  disavows the creation of any judicially enforceable procedural requirements.  Section 1231(h) unambiguously states:  “Nothing in this section shall be construed to create any substantive or procedural right or benefit that is legally enforceable by any party against the United States or its
agencies or officers or any other person.”  8  U.S.C.
1231(h).   In construing Section 1231(b)(3) as creating
certain implicit procedural rights, the First Circuit
flouted that explicit prohibition .
The First Circuit  resisted that straightforward reading of Section 1231(h), claiming that it would be anomalous for withholding -related questions not to be reviewable under the APA when they are reviewable under pe-

33

titions for review of final removal order s.  J.A. 35.  But
Congress expressly treated petitions  for review differently, by channeling all questions a rising from entry of
final removal orders into  such a petition, see 8  U.S.C.
1252(a)(5) and (b)(9), and then making clear that this includes withholding claims , subject to certain limits, see
8 U.S.C. 1252(b)(4) .  By contrast,  nothing in the APA’s
text specifically displaces Section 1231(h)’s general ban
on private enforcement of  Section 1231’s provisions.
The First Circuit also cited Zadvydas  v. Davis, 533
U.S. 678 (2001), for the proposition that Section 1231(h)
“does not bar [withholding] claims” like those here, J.A.
35.  But t here, aliens detained under Section 1231(a)
sought their release, and this Court held that Section
1231(h) does not bar a “challenge [to] detention that is
without statutory authority.”  Zadvydas , 533 U.S. at
688.  That holding is inapposite because the aliens did
not invoke any “right or benefit” allegedly created by
Section 1231 in challenging their detention  under the
habeas statute ; rather, the government raised Section
1231 as a defense to justify their continued confinement.
By contrast, respondents’ statutory claim rests on the
premise that Section 1231(b) creates enforceable procedural rights.   Put differently, if Section 1231 did not exist, respondents would have no claim, while the aliens in
Zadvydas would have had an even stronger claim.
3. The First Circuit ’s sole textual defense of  its position was to  note that Section 1231(b)(3)(C) contains
one reference to a “trier of fact.”  J.A. 31; see J.A. 106-
107.  From that, the court inferred  that the statute “contemplates” that withholding claims would be adjudicated on an “individualized basis,” where an alien would
receive “effective notice and a meaningful opportunity”
to make his case.  J.A. 31.

34

But Section 1231(b)(3)(C)’s “oblique reference” to a
trier of fact, see Johnson v. Arteaga-Martinez , 596 U.S.
573, 581 (2022), cannot bear such weight.  The provision
states that , “[i]n determining whether an alien has
demonstrated” that he would be persecuted in a country, “the trier of fact shall determine whether the alien
has sustained the alien’s burden of proof, and shall
make credibility determinations, in the manner described in [8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(1)(B)(ii) and (iii)].”  8 U.S.C.
1231(b)(3)(C).  The provision  does not , however, mandate the use of a trier of fact in the first place.
Rather, the provision, which was adopted only in
2005, merely recognized that the Executive sometimes
chooses to use a trier of fact under agency withholding
procedures, and it regulated certain evidentiary determinations  made by any such triers of fact.   See H.R.
Rep. No. 72, 109th Cong., 1st Sess. 165-167, 169 (2005).
Again, when Congress wants to actually require an individualized hearing, it does so directly and clearly.
See, e.g., 8  U.S.C. 1225(b)(1)(B)(iii)(III) .  Moreover,
where the Guidance does choose to use a trier of fact , it
complies with Section 1231(b)(3)(C), because nothing in
the Guidance prohibits an agency  trier of fact from assessing corroboration or credibility  in a manner different than under 8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(1)(B) .  J.A. 306-313.
4. The First Circuit also raised a functional argument, reasoning that the government could not effectively determine whether an alien will face persecution
without giving him “prior notice of the intended removal
destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest
that destination.”  J.A. 34; see J.A. 108-109.
But as noted, that fails as a basic matter of administrative law.  In the immigration -law context as elsewhere, the federal courts “are generally not free to im-

35

pose [additional procedural rights] if the agencies have
not chosen to grant them.”  Arteaga-Martinez , 596 U.S.
at 582 (brackets and quotation marks omitted).   In all
events, the F irst Circuit’ s criticisms fail on their own
terms because the Guidance’s procedures are more than
adequate  for the government to make the necessary determinations under Section 1231 (and CAT)  for this
class of aliens .  See Part III.C, infra.
5. Ultimately, what drove the First Circuit’s atextual holding was the perceived need to “avoid[] constitutional problems.”  J.A. 34.  But statutes need not be
construed “to eliminate all possible contentions that the
statute might be unconstitutional” where, as here, there
are no “serious constitutional doubts.”  See Reno v. Flores, 507 U.S. 292, 314 n.9 (1993); Part III.C, infra.  And
regardless, the avoidance canon is inapplicable for a
more basic reason:  “Spotting a constitutional issue does
not give a court the authority to rewrite a statute as it
pleases.”  Jennings , 583 U.S. at 298.  The constitutional -
avoidance canon permits choosing “between competing
plausible  interpretations of a statutory text.”  Ibid.  It
is not a freestanding “license to graft” entirely new procedures onto a statute’s existing text .  Ibid.; accord
Arteaga-Martinez , 596 U.S. at 581.
The First Circuit did just that.  As in Jennings ,
“[n]othing” in Section 1231(b) “even remotely supports
the imposition” of the procedures mandated  below, 583
U.S. at 847 —especially given Section 1231(h) .
B. The Guidance Does Not Violate CAT, FARRA, Or The
Implementing Regulations
1. CAT is a non -self-executing treaty in which the
United States agreed not to remove  aliens to countries
where it determines  they would face torture.   See Johnson v. Guzman Chavez , 594 U.S. 523, 530-531 (2021);

36

Medellín v. Texas, 552 U.S. 491, 520 (2008) .  FARRA is
a statute in which Congress and the President recognized that “[i]t shall be the policy of the United States
not to expel, extradite, or otherwise effect the involuntary return of any person to a country in which there
are substantial grounds for believing the person would
be in danger of being subjected to tort ure.”  §  2242(a),
112 Stat. 2681-822.  To operationalize that general policy,
FARRA tasks the Executive with promulgating “regulations to implement the obligations of the United States
under [CAT] ,” §  2242(b), 112 Stat. 2681 -822; see , e.g.,
8 C.F.R. 208.18 , 1208.18 —while barring judicial review
of the Executive’s determinations other than in a petition
for review of a final removal order, see Part I.C, supra.
Like Section 1231(b), neither CAT nor FARRA addresses, let alone mandates, procedures for complying
with the government’s obligations in the context of
third-country removals.  CAT is non -self-executing , and
FARRA’s grant of rulemaking authority  delegates procedural discretion to the Executive .  The regulations
likewise  have nothing relevant to say in the specific context of third -country removals, because they do not set
forth any process for evaluating CAT claims regarding
those new countries.  See, e.g., 8  C.F.R 208.16(f  ),
208.17(b)(2), 1208.16(f  ), 1208.17(b)(2), 1240.12(d) .
2. The First Circuit nevertheless decided to “read []”
the same notice -and-opportunity requirements that it
read into Section 1231(b) “into the relevant statutory
and regulatory provisions” of FARRA , for essentially
the same meritless reasons .  J.A. 38; see Part III.A, supra.  In so doing, it went f urther than the district court ,
which candidly admitted that there was  even “less direct, affirmative textual support” in FARRA than in
Section 1231(b) .  J.A. 110.

37

The First Circuit also reasoned that because it read
procedural requirements into Section 1231(b) for withholding claims, it must read the same requirements into
FARRA for CAT claims, because they are each governed by the same set of regulatory provisions.  J.A. 39.
That rests on two illogical bootstraps .  It incorrectly assumes the correctness of the court’s holding as to Section 1231(b), using that to justify its reconstruction of
FARRA and its regulations.  And it  lets a common set
of regulations  (for withholding and CAT) dictate the
meaning of a statute (FARRA).   In other words, even if
the First Circuit  were right about Section 1231, that
would just mean the regulations  are invalid as applied
to withholding; that would not  somehow justify judicially rewriting the regulations  and then insisting that
the same rewriting extends to FARRA , even though
that statute clearly does not  require any such thing.
Finally , the First Circuit suggested that FARRA’s
regulations require “ individualized diplomatic assurances” about specific aliens.  J.A. 32 n.14; see J.A. 126-
130.  That is incorrect .  Under applicable regulations,
the government may reject a CAT claim if it receives
reliable “assurances” “from the government of a specific country that an alien would not be tortured there if
the alien were removed to that country.”  8 C.F.R.
208.17(c), 1208.17(c).  While th e regulation s mandate
that an assurance must be “specific” to a single country
and must apply to a claim raised by “an alien,” nothing
in the regulation s requires a country’s assurance to be
alien-specific.  Ibid.  Should “the government of a specific country” give reliable “assurance s” that no alien
will be tortured in that country, that can be sufficient
for the government to conclude that any “alien would
not be tortured there if the alien were removed to that

38

country.”  Ibid.  Moreover , the First Circuit’s objection
is inapplicable on its own terms to countries without  assurance s, where the Guidance provides for individual
treatment of aliens .
C. The Guidance Does Not Violate Due Process
In all events , the re is no merit to  the constitutional
concerns that drove the decisions below —neither as independent claims nor laundered through the avoidance
canon.  The Guidance guarantees that an alien will either be sent to a country where the United States has
secured reliable assurance s that alien s will not be tortured or persecuted, or be given notice and an opportunity to raise any fears he may have regarding his
country of removal.  J.A. 306-313.  Due process requires
nothing further —even assuming that aliens somehow
can assert here a protected liberty interest in how the
United States chooses to discharge its  own obligations
under Section 1231 and CAT , notwithstanding Sections
1231(h) and 1252(a)(4) .
1. a. When the United States has obtained “credible” “assurances” from a foreign country that any “aliens removed from the United States will not be persecuted or tortured” upon removal to that country, J.A.
307, the Constitution requires no further process for aliens covered by th ose assurance s.  When the Executive
credits such an assurance , that decision is conclusive ,
see Munaf, 553 U.S. at 702-703—at least absent express
congressional authorization  for courts to review
whether the Executive complied with its own rules in
making that decision,  as in a petition for review from a
final removal order, see id. at 703 n.6.
“[I]t is for the political branches, not the Judiciary,
to assess practices in foreign countries and to determine
national policy in light of those assessments.”  Munaf,

39

553 U.S. at 700 -701.  Whe n the Executive decides torture or persecution is not “likely to result” based on
“foreign assurances it considers reliable,” the “Judiciary is not suited to second -guess such determinations —
determinations that would require federal courts to
pass judgment on foreign justice systems and undermine the Government’s ability to speak with one voice
in this area.”  Id. at 702 (quotation marks omitted).
Thus, i n Munaf, this Court held that courts could not
grant habeas relief to an American held abroad who objected that his transfer to “Iraqi custody is likely to result in torture,” explaining that the Executive had determined otherwise and that the determination  was conclusive.  Id. at 700-703; see Kiyemba v. Obama, 561 F.3d
509, 514 (D.C. Cir. 2009) (courts “may not question the
Government’s determination that a potential recipient
country is not likely to torture a detainee”) , cert. denied,
559 U.S. 1005 (2010) .
This case follows “a fortiori.”  Kiyemba, 561 F.3d at
517 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring).  Munaf involved the
transfer of Americans , whereas this case concerns the
transfer of aliens subject to final orders of removal.  In
both cases, the Judiciary lacks the expertise or authority to second -guess the Executive’s determination.
Munaf, 553 U.S. at 702.   And if that determination suffices to defeat a citizen’s  due-process claim challenging
his transfer to a given country, it necessarily suffic es to
defeat an alien’s.  See Kiyemba, 561 F.3d at 517 -518
(Kavanaugh, J., concurring) .  All the more  so where the
determination is based on a specific intergovernmental
communication —something whose credibility is especially the exclusive province of the Executive, not Judiciary, to evaluate .  See Biden v. Texas, 597 U.S. 785,
805-806 (2022).

40

b. While the district court did not dispute that foreign assurances could sometimes be sufficient, it held
that due process requires the Executive to make “an individualized determination that the foreign assurance[]
[is] sufficient” in each alien’s specific case, and that aliens are entitled to contest “the Government’s reasons
for crediting the assurances” of a given country.  J.A.
129, 133  (brackets and quotation marks omitted); see
J.A. 32 n. 15.
A federal court , however,  may not “second -guess”
the scope of the Executive’s conclusion any more than
its substance.  See Munaf, 553 U.S. at 702 -703; see also
Kiyemba , 561 F.3d at 515; id. at 517 -518 (Kavanaugh,
J., concurring).  The Judiciary is no better “suited” to
question the “foreign policy” judgment that a foreign
government’s assurance is credible when it is categorical rather than individualized.  Munaf, 553 U.S. at 702.
Indeed, Munaf itself involved a general determination :
There, the Executive credited  that the Iraqis ’ “prison
and detention facilities have generally met internationally accepted standards for basic prisoner needs.”  Ibid.
(quotation marks omitted).  None of that was prisoner -
specific; it was not even specific to torture.  If that is
enough, then so too are the assurances at issue  here—
where a country is making a specific “diplomatic assurance[]” that “aliens removed from the United States will
not be persecuted or tortured,” J.A. 307.
The district court tried to distinguish Munaf on the
ground that courts of appeals regularly review the denials of CAT or withholding claims  on review of final removal order s, meaning that such determinations must
be reviewable.  See J.A. 135-136.  That misses the point .
Although  compliance with Section 1231 and CAT is a
matter for the political branches, Congress can , in a t

41

least some circumstances,  expressly authorize judicial
review of the Executive’s compliance with its own binding regulations  in this area —as Section 1252 does
through petitions for review of final removal orders.
But the APA’s general provisions do not authorize such
review any more than the general habeas statute did in
Munaf.  553 U.S. at 703 & n.6.  Moreover, even in the
petition -for-review context, the district court did not
identify any case in which a CAT or withholding denial
was reversed because a court second -guessed the Executive’s acceptance of a foreign country’s assurances —
and it is far from clear that even Congress could authorize that scope of review in light of Executive primacy
when communicating with foreign sovereigns .
The district court also doubted that any country is
able to make a blanket assurance about how all aliens
will be treated within their borders.  See J.A. 129-130;
see also J.A. 32 n.15.  But again, that is not the district
court’s call to make.  And at any rate, the court’s skepticism is misplaced.  Both persecution and torture require
governmental involvement .  See 8 C.F.R. 208.18(a)(1) ,
1208.18(a)(1) ; cf. Matter of S -S-F-M-, 29 I.  & N. Dec.
207, 208-209 (Att’y Gen. 2025).  A foreign government is
capable of representing that such conduct will not occur
under its watch , and the United States is entitled  to
credit that assurance.
More fundamental ly, the district court’s objections
do not sound in procedural due process at all.  They instead reflect the court’s substantive view that a blanket
assurance provides an insufficient basis for the government to categorically deem a given alien not likely to be
persecuted or tortured.  This Court has rightly rejected
attempts to “recast in ‘procedural due process’ terms”
what is really a challenge to the “  ‘substantive’  ” criteria

42

the government has adopted.  Flores, 507 U.S. at 308
(refuting  similar argument for “individual[ized]” procedure).  It makes no sense to require the government to
provide additional process with respect to potential evidence that is immaterial  under the relevant substantive
standard.  When the government is satisfied  based on
foreign assurances that no  alien will be persecuted or
tortured in the receiving country, the Due Process
Clause does not further require a pointless “individualized determination .”  Olim v. Wakinekona , 461 U.S.
238, 250 (1983)  (“Process is not an end in itself ,” and a
plaintiff has no “right to demand needless formality. ”).
2. a. For aliens not subject to a countrywide assurance, the Guidance is also constitutional .  Due process
at most requires “notice reasonably calculated, under
all the circumstances, to apprise the interested parties
of the pendency of the action and afford them an opportunity to present their objections .”  Mullane v. Central
Hanover Bank & Trust Co. , 339 U.S. 306, 31 4 (1950).  In
applying that standard, “it must weigh heavily in the
balance that control over matters of immigration is a
sovereign prerogative, largely within the control of the
Executive and the Legislature.”  Plasencia , 459 U.S. at
34; accord Demore v. Kim, 538 U.S. 510, 52 1-522 (2003).
The Guidance easily satisfies any minimal requirements of due process in this context .  It provides that
aliens will receive personal notice of the proposed country of removal —which will be “read to the alien in a language he or she understands.”  J.A. 311.  The Guidance
thus guarantees actual notice to every affected alien.
Cf. Dusenbery v. United States , 534 U.S. 161, 167-168
(2002).  Moreover, once an alien receives notice, he is
given a reasonable period of time to voice a fear of
removal—generally 24 hours, or once given a “reasona-

43

ble means and opportunity to speak with an attorney
prior to removal.”  J.A. 311.  Should the alien affirmatively state such a fear, he is supplied “an opportunity
to present [his] objections” to  an asylum officer .  Mullane, 339 U.S. at 313; see J.A. 312.  DHS “will generally
screen the alien within 24 hours of referral,” and if it
finds the alien has shown he “would more likely than
not” be tortured or persecuted on removal, the alien will
be referred to full administrative proceedings.  Ibid.
The Constitution does not require more.
b. The district court’s objections lack merit.
The district court first insisted that 24 hours is
too short a time for aliens to voice a fear of removal.
See J.A. 125 n.86.  But that timing is similar to the
expedited -removal process this Court upheld against a
due-process challenge in DHS v. Thuraissigiam , 591
U.S. 103 (2020).  That process allows removal “without
further hearing or review,” 8  U.S.C. 1225(b)(1)(A)(i),
subject only to a limited window to establish a “credible
fear of persecution,” Thuraissigiam , 591 U.S. at 109.
And if an immigration  officer determines  the alien does
not have a credible fear, the immigration judge’s  review
is to be “concluded as expeditiously as possible” and
“to the maximum extent practicable within 24 hours” —
and “in no case l ater than 7 days  after” the no -credible -
fear determination.   8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(1)(B)(iii)(III).
The expedited -removal statute does not limit the countries to which an alien can be removed under Section
1231(b), see 8  U.S.C. 1225(b) (1), so aliens processed for
expedited removal who are to be removed somewhere
other than their home country are subject to the se same
procedures for raising and assessing fear -of-persecution claims, see, e.g., 8 U.S.C. 1231(b).

44

Neither the district court nor respondents have explained why those sorts of procedures are constitutionally adequate for expedited removal, but not here.  If
anything, the Guidance involves an even better case for
expedition.  The class comprises aliens who already
have final orders of removal and have had a prior opportunity to raise withholding or CAT claims (and in many
cases, have successfully done so); they are  thus familiar
with th ose modes of protection , and are generally able
to raise them promptly if merited.   Moreover, expedition is especially appropriate in the third -country context, where delays from additional review conflict with
the speed often needed to effectively execute on arrangements with foreign countries .  See, e.g., C.A. Doc.
118413581, at 3-4.  In fact, th ose countries  are ones
where an alien is particularly unlikely to have a viable
claim of torture or persecution :  both require extreme
abuse, with the government’s involvement, going well
beyond ordinary violence or crime , see pp. 6-7, 42 , supra, and aliens are unlikely to suffer that type of mistreatment in foreign countries where  they lack prior
connections.
The district court also objected to the fact that the
Guidance requir es an alien to show that it is “more
likely than not” he is entitled to protection , because that
standard is more demanding than what an alien must
typically show during a credible -fear interview ( at least
a “significant possibility ,” 8 C.F.R. 208.30(e), 1208.30(e)).
See J.A. 125 n.86.  But the preponderance standard is
the same standard that an alien ultimately must satisfy
to obtain relief on the merits , see 8 C.F.R. 208.16(b)  and
(c)(2), 1208.16(b) and (c)(2), and it does not  violate due
process to require the alien to satisfy that standard under the record compiled during an initial review in order

45

to obtain further administrative proceedings  that might
involve an expanded record.
The district court also took issue with the Guidance ’s
requiring an alien to “affirmatively state” a fear of removal and direct ing immigration officers “not” to “affirmatively ask whether the alien is afraid of being removed to the country of removal.”  J.A. 125 (emphasis
omitted).  But due process requires only an “opportunity” for the affected party to “present their objections.”  Mullane, 339 U.S. 314.  It does not require the
government to solicit those objections , or offer the full
menu of options .  Indeed, immigration law generally
places the onus upon the alien .  See, e.g., 8  U.S.C.
1225(b)(1)(A)(ii).
That policy decision makes good sense.  Th at aspect
of the Guidance was adopted because DHS concluded
that affirmatively asking an alien whether he feared removal would yield an excessive number of false -positive
answers.  See J.A. 307.  The Biden Administration drew
the same commonsense conclusion and adopted a similar practice in the expedited -removal context .  89 Fed.
Reg. 48,710, 48,740, 48,743 (June 7, 2024).  That reasonable judgment fits well within the discretion the Due
Process Clause affords in the immigration space.
3. Finally, t he lower courts’ decision to augment the
Guidance on a classwide basis is especially misguided
because many class members have no due -process
rights beyond what the political branches have chosen
to provide with respect to  executing their  removal.
This Court has long held that the “due process rights
of an alien seeking initial entry” are no greater than
“[w]hatever the procedure[s] authorized by Congress.”
Thuraissigiam , 591 U.S. at 139.  For aliens who have
never been admitted —a group that includes the many

46

class members here  who were ordered removed as inadmissible rather than deportable , see J.A. 247; see also
Blanche v. Lau, 609 U.S. 1, 5 (2026) —“the decisions of
executive or administrative officers, acting within powers expressly conferred by Congress, are due process of
law,” Nishimura Ekiu  v. United States , 142 U.S. 651,
660 (1892).
This Court has applied that principle beyond aliens
stopped literally at the border.  Thuraissigiam , 591
U.S. at 138 -140.  For instance, this Court has long employed the “entry fiction” that “aliens who arrive at
ports of entry  *  * *  are ‘treated’ for due process purposes ‘as if stopped at the border, ’ ” even for “those paroled elsewhere in the country for years pending removal.”  Id. at 139 ; see, e.g., Kaplan v. Tod, 267 U.S.
228, 230 (1925).
Aliens who evade detection in crossing the border,
and never receive sovereign permission to remain in the
country, do not obtain greater rights than those stopped
at the border in the first place.  As this Court has observed, “the deportation of an alien who is found to be
here in violation of law is not a deprivation of liberty
without due process of law.”  United States ex rel.
Turner v. Williams , 194 U.S. 279, 290 (1904).  An alien
“does not become one of the people to whom these
things are secured by our Constitution by an attempt to
enter forbidden by law.”  Id. at 292; accord Carlson v.
Landon, 342 U.S. 524, 534 & n.18 (1952); cf. Fong Yue
Ting v. United States , 149 U.S. 698, 724 (1893).
It would be perverse  for an unlawful entrant who violates our laws and evades detection to receive better
constitutional treatment than someone who presents at
the border and is paroled into the country (perhaps
even for decades).  The Due Process Clause does not of-

47

fer such  unjust enrichment to those who successfully
breach this Nation’s borders against our laws.  Congress has reached a similar conclusion , deeming any alien present in the United States without admission to
be an applicant for admission .  See 8  U.S.C. 1225(a)(1).
By contrast, “once an alien gains admission to our country and begins to develop the ties that go with permanent residence,” “his constitutional status changes accordingly.”  Plasencia , 459 U.S. at 32; accord Wong
Yang Sung  v. McGrath, 339 U.S. 33, 49 -50 (1950).
The district court  tried to frame this Court’s precedents as drawing a line not between aliens admitted and
not admitted, but between aliens apprehended at the
border and those who make it into the interior .  See J.A.
115-117.  That is unsound.  In Thuraissigiam , after all,
the alien made it past the border  (albeit only by 25
yards).  591 U.S. at 138-140.  So have parolees.  See, e.g.,
Shaughnessy  v. United States ex rel. Mezei , 345 U.S.
206, 214 -215 (1953).   And Congress has imposed no geographic limit on when applicants for admission may be
subject to expedited removal.  8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(1)(A)(iii)
(authorizing government to apply expedited removal to
any alien who has not been admitted or paroled and has
not “ been physically present in the United States continuously for the 2 -year period immediately prior”).
Mere physical presence in the Nation has never been
the test.  See, e.g., Nishimura Ekiu , 142 U.S. at 660; see
also, e.g., Rodriguez  v. Vergara, No. 26 -50183 (5th Cir.
Oct. 23, 2026) (en banc), slip op. 11 -15.
Of course , once an alien is physically present within
the United States, the Due Process Clause applies.  See
Plyler v. Doe, 457 U.S. 202, 215 (1982).  But what due
process requires, and whether it may be more than
whatever the political branches have decided to provide ,

48

turns on the governmental action at issue.  Cf. Kim, 538
U.S. at 521 -523.  For illegal aliens who have final removal orders and were never admitted , due process
does not license courts to superintend how the political
branches execute their removal.  See  Thuraissigiam ,
591 U.S. at 139 ; cf. AADC, 525 U.S. at 491 -492;
Zadvydas , 533 U.S. at 703 -704 (Scalia, J., dissenting).
The process due is what ever the political branches provide.  Here, that is the Guidance.
CONCLUSION
The court of appeals ’ judgment should be  reversed .
Respectfully submitted.

Implementation of the Convention  Against Torture.
(a) Definitions .  The definitions in this  subsection
incorporate the definition  of torture contained in Article
1 of the  Convention Against Torture, subject to  the reservations, understandings, declarations,  and provisos
contained in  the United States Senate resolution of  ratification of the Convention.
(1) Torture is defined as any act by  which severe
pain or suffering, whether  physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted  on a person for such purposes as  obtaining from him or her or a third  person information or
a confession,  punishing him or her for an act he or  she
or a third person has committed or  is suspected of having committed, or  intimidating or coercing him or her or
a third person, or for any reason based  on discrimination
of any kind, when  such pain or suffering is inflicted by
or at the instigation of or with the consent  or acquiescence of a public official  acting in an official capacity or
other person acting in an official capacity.   Pain or suffering inflicted by a public  official who is not acting under color of  law shall not constitute pain or suffering  inflicted by or at the instigation  of or with the consent or
acquiescence  of a public official acting in an official  capacity or other person acting in an  official capacity, alt-

39a

hough a different  public official acting in an official capacity or other person acting in an official  capacity could
instigate, consent  to, or acquiesce in the pain or suffering inflicted by the public official who is  not acting under
color of law.
(2) Torture is an extreme form of  cruel and inhuman
treatment and does  not include lesser forms of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment  that do
not amount to torture.
(3) Torture does not include pain or  suffering arising only from, inherent in  or incidental to lawful sanctions.  Lawful sanctions include judicially imposed  sanctions and other enforcement  actions authorized by law,
including  the death penalty, but do not include  sanctions
that defeat the object and  purpose of the Convention
Against Torture  to prohibit torture.
(4) In order to constitute torture,  mental pain or
suffering must be prolonged  mental harm caused by or
resulting  from:
(i) The intentional infliction or  threatened infliction
of severe physical  pain or suffering;
(ii) The administration or application,  or threatened
administration or application, of mind altering substances
or other procedures calculated  to disrupt profoundly the
senses or the  personality;
(iii) The threat of imminent death; or
(iv) The threat that another person  will imminently
be subjected to death,  severe physical pain or suffering,
or the administration or application of mind  altering substances or other procedures calculated to disrupt pro -
foundly the  sense or personality.

40a

(5) In order to constitute torture, an  act must be
specifically intended to inflict  severe physical or mental
pain or  suffering.  An act that results in unanticipated
or unintended severity of  pain and suffering is not torture.
(6) In order to constitute torture an  act must be directed against a person  in the offender ’s custody or
physical  control.
(7) Acquiescence of a public official  requires that
the public official, prior  to the activity constituting torture, have awareness of such activity and  thereafter
breach his or her legal responsibility  to intervene to prevent such activity.  Such awareness requires  a finding
of either actual knowledge or  willful blindness.   Willful
blindness  means that the public official acting in  an official capacity or other person  acting in an official capacity
was aware of a high probability of activity  constituting
torture and deliberately  avoided learning the truth; it is
not enough that such public official acting  in an official
capacity or other person  acting in an official capacity
was mistaken,  recklessly disregarded the  truth, or negligently failed to inquire.   In order for a public official to
breach his or her legal responsibility to intervene  to prevent activity constituting  torture, the official must have
been charged with preventing the activity as  part of his
or her duties and have failed  to intervene.   No person
will be deemed  to have breached a legal responsibility  to
intervene if such person is unable to  intervene, or if the
person intervenes  but is unable to prevent the activity
that constitutes torture.
(8) Noncompliance with applicable  legal procedural
standards does not per se constitute torture.

10. 8 C.F.R. 1208.18 provides:
Implementation of the Convention  Against Torture.
(a) Definitions .  The definitions in this  subsection
incorporate the definition  of torture contained in Article
1 of the  Convention Against Torture, subject to  the reservations, understandings, declarations,  and provisos
contained in  the United States Senate resolution of  ratification of the Convention.
(1) Torture is defined as any act by  which severe
pain or suffering, whether  physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted  on a person for such purposes as  obtaining from him or her or a third  person information or
a confession,  punishing him or her for an act he or  she

59a

or a third person has committed or  is suspected of having committed, intimidating  or coercing him or her or a
third person, or for any reason based on  discrimination
of any kind, when such  pain or suffering is inflicted by,
or at  the instigation of, or with the consent  or acquiescence of, a public official acting  in an official capacity or
other person  acting in an official capacity.  Pain or suffering inflicted by a public official  who is not acting under color of  law shall not constitute pain or suffering  inflicted by, or at the instigation  of, or with the consent or
acquiescence  of, a public official acting in an  official
capacity or other person acting  in an official capacity,
although a different  public official acting in an official
capacity or other person acting in  an official capacity
could instigate,  consent to, or acquiesce in the pain or
suffering inflicted by the public official  who is not acting
under color of law.
(2) Torture is an extreme form of  cruel and inhuman
treatment and does  not include lesser forms of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment  that do
not amount to torture.
(3) Torture does not include pain or  suffering arising only from, inherent in  or incidental to lawful sanctions.  Lawful sanctions include judicially imposed  sanctions and other enforcement  actions authorized by law,
including  the death penalty, but do not include  sanctions
that defeat the object and  purpose of the Convention
Against Torture  to prohibit torture.
(4) In order to constitute torture,  mental pain or
suffering must be prolonged  mental harm caused by or
resulting  from:

60a

(i) The intentional infliction or  threatened infliction
of severe physical  pain or suffering;
(ii) The administration or application,  or threatened
administration or application, of mind altering substances
or other procedures calculated  to disrupt profoundly the
senses or the  personality;
(iii) The threat of imminent death; or
(iv) The threat that another person  will imminently
be subjected to death,  severe physical pain or suffering,
or the  administration or application of mind  altering
substances or other procedures  calculated to disrupt
profoundly the  sense or personality.
(5) In order to constitute torture, an  act must be
specifically intended to inflict  severe physical or mental
pain or  suffering.  An act that results in unanticipated
or unintended severity of  pain and suffering is not torture.
(6) In order to constitute torture an  act must be directed against a person  in the offender ’s custody or
physical  control.
(7) Acquiescence of a public official  requires that
the public official, prior  to the activity constituting torture, have awareness of such activity and  thereafter
breach his or her legal responsibility  to intervene to prevent such activity.  Such awareness requires  a finding of
either actual knowledge or willful blindness.  Willful blindness means that the public official acting in  an official
capacity or other person  acting in an official capacity
was aware of a high probability of activity  constituting
torture and deliberately  avoided learning the truth; it is
not enough that such public official acting  in an official

61a

capacity or other person  acting in an official capacity
was mistaken,  recklessly disregarded the  truth, or negligently failed to inquire.   In order for a public official to
breach his or her legal responsibility to intervene  to prevent activity constituting  torture, the official must have
been charged with preventing the activity as  part of his
or her duties and have failed  to intervene.  No person
will be deemed  to have breached a legal responsibility  to
intervene if such person is unable to  intervene, or if the
person intervenes  but is unable to prevent the activity
that constitutes torture.
(8) Noncompliance with applicable  legal procedural
standards does not per se constitute torture.

11. 8 C.F.R. 1240.12  provides:
Decision of the immigration  judge.
(a) Contents .  The decision of the immigration  judge
may be oral or written.   The decision of the immigration
judge shall include a finding as to inadmissibility  or deportability.   The formal  enumeration of findings is not
required.   The decision shall also contain  reasons for
granting or denying the request.   The decision shall be
concluded  with the order of the immigration  judge.

(b) Summary decision .  Notwithstanding  the provisions of paragraph  (a) of this section, in any case where
inadmissibility or deportability is determined  on the
pleadings pursuant to  § 1240.10(b) and the respondent
does not  make an application under § 1240.11, the alien
is statutorily ineligible for relief,  or the respondent applies for voluntary  departure only and the immigration
judge grants the application, the immigration  judge may
enter a summary decision  or, if voluntary departure is
granted, a summary decision with an  alternate order of
removal.
(c) Order of the immigration judge .  The order of
the immigration judge shall  direct the respondent ’s removal from  the United States, or the termination of the
proceedings, or other such disposition  of the case as may
be appropriate.   The immigration judge is authorized  to
issue orders in the alternative  or in combination as he or
she may deem necessary.
(d) Removal .  When a respondent is ordered  removed from the United States,  the immigration judge
shall identify a  country, or countries in the alternative,
to which the alien ’s removal  may in the first instance be
made, pursuant  to the provisions of section 241(b)  of the
Act.  In the event that the Department  of Homeland Security is unable  to remove the alien to the specified  or
alternative country or countries,  the order of the immigration judge does not limit the authority of  the Department of Homeland Security  to remove the alien to any
other country  as permitted by section 241(b) of  the Act.
